topic_info.title: Care for patients who identify as transgender

list.listitem: Patients who are diagnosed with gender incongruence and/or gender dysphoria may not desire hormone therapy but those who are treated with hormone therapy have an improved sense of self and decreased anxiety as well as less dysphoria. B

Hormone therapy consisting of estrogen or testosterone for the management of patients with gender dysphoria/incongruence has a low risk of negative outcomes when treated by an experienced physician. B

Surgical management (gender reassignment surgery, breast surgery, or chest surgery) for patients with gender dysphoria/incongruence does not significantly resolve the individual's dysphoria; however, there is typically satisfaction with the cosmetic result. B
The patient's physician and mental health provider should discuss and provide options for individuals who desire future fertility prior to initiating hormone therapy. C

background.definition: An individual who identifies as transgender is someone who does not identify with the gender assigned at birth. Individuals who do not experience anxiety regarding their gender identity and difference from gender assigned at birth are described as having “gender incongruence”. “Gender dysphoria” is defined as an individual who experiences distress or anxiety regarding the incongruence of their gender assigned at birth and their gender identity. This definition is outlined in the DSM-5 and adults must have experienced distress or anxiety for at least six months.

list.listitem: The prevalence of persons identifying as transgender is 0.6% of the US population; however these data are based on self-reporting and have limitations based on the individual choosing to or not to report.
Currently there are an estimated 1.4 million adults and 150,000 youth living in the United States who identify as transgender.
Gender dysphoria is a condition defined by DSM-5 regarding individuals who do not identify with the gender assigned at birth and have associated distress or anxiety. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Distress and anxiety associated with preoccupation with one or more perceived physical flaws/defects/abnormalities that is often not seen/noticed by others or is considered minor by others. This leads to social, occupational, and interpersonal functioning impairments.
A persistent desire of an able-bodied individual to have a physical disability such as an amputation of a limb(s) or paraplegia. Individuals often seek out surgical amputations or dangerous methods.
A persistent desire to undergo castration and/or penectomy unrelated to gender identity.

list.listitem: Gender dysphoria is diagnosed based on the DSM-5, which states that for a person to be diagnosed with gender dysphoria there must be a marked difference between the individual's expressed or experienced gender and the gender assigned at birth, and it must continue for at least six months. In children, the desire to be of the other gender must be present and verbalized. This condition must also cause clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning to be classified as gender dysphoria.
Medical professionals can identify individuals who are transgender through a sexual orientation and gender identity (SO/GI) history.
There is no specific physical examination needed to make the diagnosis of gender dysphoria. Rather, the physical exam should be based on the specific needs of the patient at time of the visit.
Chest and genitourinary exam is only needed based on the patient's concern, should be chaperoned, and should be stopped if the patient experiences discomfort.
Physicians should use a culturally sensitive, trauma-informed approach to the care of transgender patients.
Mental health evaluation is not required, but mental health comorbidities are common and should be screened for, as they can impact treatment.
Physicians should work collaboratively with mental health professionals if needed.

Patients who are diagnosed with gender dysphoria/incongruence may not desire hormone therapy but those who are treated with hormone therapy have an improved sense of self and decreased anxiety and dysphoria. B
Gender affirming hormone therapy with estrogen or testosterone has a low risk of negative outcomes when treated by an experienced physician. B

Patients who are diagnosed with gender incongruence or gender dysphoria may not desire hormone therapy. Patients who desire hormone therapy and are able to access it have an improved sense of self and decreased anxiety as well as less dysphoria.
Gender affirming hormone therapy is recommended only for patients whose gender incongruence and gender dysphoria is marked and persistent.

The process of initiating hormone therapy includes evaluating the patient and noting sustained gender dysphoria or gender incongruence. The patient should have capacity to make informed choices. Any co-existing medical and mental health conditions should be well controlled.
Patients should understand the reversible and irreversible effects on physical appearance, future fertility, and social impacts, as well as the risks and benefits of hormone therapy.
The patient's physician should discuss fertility goals and provide options for individuals who desire future fertility prior to initiating hormone therapy.
Informed consent should be obtained prior to initiating gender affirming hormone therapy.
Gender affirming hormone therapy with estrogen or testosterone has a low risk of negative outcomes when treated by an experienced physician.
Masculinizing hormone therapy consists of testosterone given transdermally or by injection. Intramuscular and subcutaneous injections are equally effective..
Testosterone enanthate and cypionate are dosed initially at 50 mg IM or SQ every week or 100 mg every two weeks. Another option is topical/transdermal testosterone 1.6% gel 50-100 mg applied daily..

Testosterone stimulates erythropoiesis with a subsequent increase in the hemoglobin and hematocrit. There is a potential development of polycythemia in transgender male patients, particularly in patients with obstructive sleep apnea (see ).

Recommended follow-up for individuals on hormone therapy is every three months for the first year and every six months thereafter. Follow-up is to evaluate for potential adverse reactions to hormone therapy as well as to assess the effectiveness of therapy. The patient should have labs drawn to evaluate their testosterone level as well as hemoglobin and hematocrit. Total testosterone range is 320-1,000 ng/dL with a target level of 400-700 ng/dL.

Feminizing hormone therapy consists of estrogen administered transdermally, by injection or orally. Ethinyl estradiol carries a 6-8% risk of venous thrombosis compared with 17 β-estradiol and is therefore avoided for feminizing hormone therapy.

Dosing options include estradiol 2-6 mg/day orally, estradiol patch 0.025-0.2 mg/day (changing the patch every 3-5 days), estradiol valerate 5-30 mg IM every 2 weeks, or estradiol cypionate 2-5 mg IM once weekly.

Estradiol use among transgender women has a risk of venous thrombosis, which varies based on different research studies as well as the route of administration (oral, intramuscular, or transdermal). In a cross-sectional study that included 214 transgender women compared with a control group of 619 cisgender women and 640 cisgender men, 5% developed a deep venous thrombosis and/or pulmonary embolism within the first year of therapy. Tobacco smoking was the main risk factor. Another study had an incidence of 6.4% for venous thromboembolism over the 12-month follow-up period, but that was observed among the use of ethinyl estradiol, which is currently not the chosen hormone formulation due to this risk (see ).
Antiandrogens can be used in conjunction with estrogen therapy, specifically spironolactone. Spironolactone inhibits testosterone secretion and acts to block the androgen receptor.

A single-blinded trial of 52 transgender women randomized them to estradiol valerate 4 mg/day plus spironolactone 100 mg/day versus estradiol valerate 4 mg/day plus cyproterone acetate 25 mg/day. Cyproterone acetate was more effective at lowering testosterone level than spironolactone (90% vs 19% p value <0.001). However, cyproterone acetate had serious adverse side effects consisting of drug-induced liver injury and asymptomatic hyperprolactinemia. Cyproterone acetate is widely used in Europe but is not available in the US, where spironolactone is used for androgen blocking.

Recommended follow-up for individuals on hormone therapy is every three months for the first year and every six months thereafter. Follow-up is to evaluate for potential adverse reactions to hormone therapy as well as to assess the effectiveness of therapy. The targeted estradiol level range is 100 to 200 pg/mL and a total testosterone level less than 50 ng/dL. Patients who are taking spironolactone should a serum potassium and kidney function checked every three months for the first year and then annually..

Fewer than half of transgender patients pursue gender-affirming surgery. It is more common in transmasculine patients. Some patients do not pursue it out of preference and others encounter barriers such as cost or availability of surgeons.
Patients are generally recommended to complete at least 6 months of gender-affirming hormone therapy prior to considering gender affirming surgery.

Surgery can also help with the management of the patient's gender dysphoria. Surgical procedures for male-to-female patients consists of breast/chest surgery (augmentation mammoplasty) and genital surgery (penectomy, orchiectomy, vaginoplasty clitoroplasty, and vulvoplasty).
Other surgical options include facial feminization surgery, liposuction, lipofilling, thyroid cartilage reduction, hair reconstruction, or gluteal augmentation.

Surgical options for female-to-male patients consist of breast/chest surgery (mastectomy) and genital surgery (hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, metoidioplasty, phalloplasty, vaginectomy, and scrotoplasty).
